01.note: Rabbi Zeira says that last night Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, appeared to him in a dream. Rabbi Zeira asked whom he was placed near in the upper realms. Rabbi Yosei said near Rabbi Yoḥanan, who is near Rabbi Yannai, who is near Rabbi Ḥanina, who is near Rabbi Ḥiyya. When Rabbi Zeira asked why Rabbi Yoḥanan was not placed near Rabbi Ḥiyya, Rabbi Yosei answered: in a place of fiery sparks and burning fires, who could bring Rabbi Yoḥanan, son of Nappaḥa, there?
01.why: The Gemara has been praising Rabbi Ḥiyya, whose deeds Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called greater than his own; this dream places Rabbi Ḥiyya at the head of the heavenly order, beyond even great Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Has the dream and tells it.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Appears in the dream and describes where the Sages are placed in heaven.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Called son of Nappaḥa; Rabbi Yosei is placed near him, but he cannot be brought near Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Stands at the head of the chain, in a place of fiery sparks and burning fires.

terms.meaning: The world to come, where the souls of the righteous dwell after death.

02.note: Rav Ḥaviva passes on what Rav Ḥaviva bar Surmakei told him. He saw a Sage whom Elijah the prophet used to visit, whose eyes looked healthy in the morning but charred by fire in the evening. The Sage explained that he had asked Elijah to show him the Sages rising to the heavenly academy. Elijah let him look at all of them except the chariot of Rabbi Ḥiyya, the one chariot that rises and descends on its own, without angels. He could not restrain himself and looked; two fiery flames struck him and blinded him. The next day he prostrated himself on Rabbi Ḥiyya's burial cave, saying that he studies Rabbi Ḥiyya's teachings, and he was healed.
02.why: It is the next in a run of stories praising Rabbi Ḥiyya: after a dream that ranks him above other Sages in heaven, this one shows his heavenly chariot is too holy even to look at.

people.name: Rav Ḥaviva
people.about: Reports the story.

people.name: Rav Ḥaviva bar Surmakei
people.about: Told Rav Ḥaviva about the Sage he saw.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who visited the Sage and showed him the Sages ascending to heaven.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: The Sage whose chariot no one may gaze on; the blinded Sage prays at his burial cave.

terms.meaning: The house of study in heaven where, in these stories, the souls of the Sages go on learning Torah.
Teachings from the early Sages that were not included in the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law. Rabbi Ḥiyya was known for gathering them.

03.note: Elijah the prophet often came to the academy of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, but one New Moon he was late. He explained that he had to wake Abraham, wash his hands, wait for him to pray and lay him down again, and then do the same for Isaac and for Jacob; woken together, their prayers would bring the Messiah before his time. Asked whether anyone alive was like them, Elijah named Rabbi Ḥiyya and his sons. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi decreed a fast and had them lead the prayer: at 'Who makes the wind blow' the wind blew, at 'Who makes the rain fall' rain fell, and as they came to 'Who revives the dead' the world trembled. In heaven Elijah was found to have revealed the secret and beaten with sixty fiery lashes. He came down as a bear of fire and distracted the people.
03.why: The Gemara is still praising Rabbi Ḥiyya, here as a man whose prayer could rival the Patriarchs', and it continues a series of stories about Elijah and the Sages.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, a regular at Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's academy, who tends to the Patriarchs and gives away the secret about Rabbi Ḥiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Head of the academy; he asks Elijah why he was late and decrees the fast.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: With his sons, the one Elijah names as equal to the Patriarchs in prayer.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: With Isaac and Jacob, the Patriarch whom Elijah wakes to pray, one at a time.

terms.meaning: The first day of a month in the Jewish calendar, marked with special prayers.
The central standing prayer of every Jewish service. Its second blessing praises God who makes the wind blow, makes the rain fall and revives the dead.
Called a public fast day, when the community gathered to pray and someone was chosen to lead them.

04.note: Shmuel Yarḥina’a was the physician of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had pain in his eye, he refused to have medicine put in it, and refused a salve too, saying he could not bear either. So Shmuel put the medicine in a tube of herbs under his pillow, and he was healed. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tried to ordain him as a rabbi, but it never worked out. Shmuel told him not to be upset: he had seen the book of Adam, the first man, and it said that Shmuel Yarḥina’a would be called a wise man but not rabbi, and that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's healing would come through him. It also said that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Natan are the end of the Mishna, and Rav Ashi and Ravina the end of instruction.
04.why: It belongs to a chain of stories about the great Sages, following tales of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Elijah, and its closing line about Rav Ashi and Ravina leads the Gemara to a verse from Psalms used as a memory aid.

people.name: Shmuel Yarḥina’a
people.about: Physician of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who heals his eye and is never ordained.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; Shmuel's patient, who tries to ordain him.

terms.meaning: To give someone the formal title of rabbi and the authority that goes with it.
The first great written collection of Jewish law, which the Talmud discusses.
Here, the last of the Sages whose teaching makes up the Talmud itself.

05.note: Rabba bar Naḥmani was accused at the king's palace of keeping 12,000 Jews from the king's head tax for a month each summer and winter. He fled. A royal messenger reached his inn and his face was turned backward; Rabba had it healed, and the messenger found him. Locked in a room, Rabba prayed, the wall crumbled, and he fled to a swamp to study. In heaven God said a doubtful case of leprosy was pure and the whole academy said impure; they sent for Rabba to decide. The Angel of Death could not reach him while he studied, until a wind in the reeds sounded like soldiers and he asked to die rather than be handed over. He died saying 'Pure, pure.' Abaye, Rava and the Sages found his body under hovering birds and mourned him seven days.
05.why: The Gemara tells it as another story about the greatness of the Sages, after its tales of Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

people.name: Rabba bar Naḥmani
people.about: The Sage accused before the king; he says he is preeminent in the laws of leprosy and of tents.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Reports the story.

people.name: Rav Ḥama, son of the daughter of Ḥasa
people.about: Told the story to Rav Kahana.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who rules the doubtful case pure against the rest of the heavenly academy.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: With Rava and the other Sages, goes out to bury Rabba bar Naḥmani.

terms.meaning: A tax paid to the king by each man. Rabba's accusers said the men who came to study with him for a month at a time were not paying it.
A bright white spot on the skin, one of the signs of the biblical skin disease often translated leprosy; whether it or a white hair came first decides if the person is ritually impure.
A voice from heaven that speaks aloud, here to praise Rabba as he dies.
Formally shunned by the community, a punishment the Sages could impose.

06.note: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya told his son to go out and hire workers for them. The son hired them and promised to provide their food, without saying how much. When he came back and told his father, Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya said: My son, even if you made them a feast like King Solomon's in his time, you would not have fulfilled your duty to them, because they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
06.why: The mishna says workers' meals follow local custom, so the Gemara asks how this incident fits. It answers that the mishna is incomplete: an employer who promises food takes on more than custom, and this incident shows it.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya
people.about: The employer, who sends his son to hire workers and warns him what his promise means.

terms.meaning: A passage of the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law, which the Gemara then discusses.

07.note: A shepherd was grazing animals on the bank of the Pappa River when one of them slipped and fell into the water. He came before Rabba, who exempted him from paying, saying: What could he have done?
07.why: The Gemara is discussing the four kinds of people who guard others' property, and this case opens its debate on how much care a paid guardian owes: Rabba says only what people usually give, and Abaye challenges him.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The judge who frees the shepherd from paying.

terms.meaning: Someone paid to look after another's property, such as a hired shepherd. He must pay for theft or loss, but not for accidents beyond his control.

08.note: Bar Adda the porter was taking animals across the narrow bridge of Neresh when one pushed another into the water. Rav Pappa held him liable. Bar Adda asked: What should I have done? Rav Pappa said: You should have taken them across one by one. Bar Adda answered: Do you know of your sister's son who could take them across one by one? Rav Pappa replied that people long before him had already complained about this, and no one had paid attention to them.
08.why: Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna have just rejected Rabba's view, holding that a paid guardian owes extra care; Rav Pappa's ruling holds the porter to that higher standard.

people.name: Bar Adda the porter
people.about: Hired to move the animals across the bridge.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge who holds him liable.

09.note: Aivu left flax for safekeeping in the house of Ronya. A man named Shabbu came and snatched it. In the end the thief was identified. The case came before Rav Naḥman, who held the guardian liable.
09.why: The Gemara asks whether Rav Naḥman disagrees with Rav Huna bar Avin, who let an unpaid guardian choose between swearing an oath and suing an identified thief. Rava answers that government men stood nearby, so the guardian could have shouted for help.

people.name: Aivu
people.about: Owner of the flax, who deposited it.

people.name: Ronya
people.about: The flax was kept in Ronya's house.

people.name: Shabbu
people.about: The thief who snatched the flax.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who holds the guardian liable.

10.note: Mareimar bar Ḥanina rented a mule to people of Bei Ḥozai and went out to load it with them. They were negligent with it and it died. Rava held them liable. The Sages told Rava this was negligence while the owner was with the animal, which frees the renters, and Rava was embarrassed. In the end it came out that Mareimar had gone out only to supervise the loading, so Rava's ruling stood. The Gemara then asks why Rava was embarrassed, since some Sages would hold the renters liable even so, and it retells the case: the mule was stolen and died in the thief's house, and the same exchange followed.
10.why: Rava has just taught that borrowing from someone while he works for you counts as borrowing together with the owner, which frees the borrower; this case turns on whether the owner was really working with the animal.

people.name: Mareimar bar Ḥanina
people.about: Owner of the mule, who rented it out and went along at the loading.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge, embarrassed by the Sages' objection until the facts came out.

terms.meaning: A rule that if the owner is working for the borrower or renter at the time he lends the animal, the borrower does not pay for what happens to it.

11.note: A man came before Rav after someone had planted trees in his field without permission. Rav told him to have the planter's costs and the gain to the field appraised, and later added that the planter would get the lesser amount. Both times the owner said: I do not want them. In the end Rav saw that the owner had fenced the field and was guarding the trees. Rav told him he had shown he was pleased with them, so the planter would get the greater amount.
11.why: Rav and Shmuel disagree on how to pay someone who plants another's field without permission; the Gemara explains that Rav's view was never stated outright but inferred from this case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The judge, who changes his ruling once he sees the owner guarding the trees.

terms.meaning: Have the court work out two figures, what the planter spent and how much the trees added to the field's value. Paying the lesser favors the owner; paying the greater favors the planter.

12.note: A man bought a boatload of wine and could not find a place to store it. He asked a woman whether she had a place to rent him, and she said no. So he betrothed her, and she gave him a place for the wine. He went home, wrote her a bill of divorce and sent it to her. She hired porters, paid them out of the wine itself, and had the wine taken out and put on the road. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, quoted a verse: As he did, so shall be done to him; his repayment shall come back on his own head.
12.why: The Gemara has been asking when a landlord may put out a tenant without notice; it goes on to explain that this woman could refuse to house a man who had deceived her, even if her place was for rent.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Judges the case and approves what the woman did.

terms.meaning: Performed the first stage of Jewish marriage, which makes a couple legally married even before the wedding.
The written document, called a get, by which a man ends a marriage.

13.note: The people of Alexandria would betroth their wives, and when the women were about to enter the wedding canopy, other men would come and snatch them away. The Sages wanted to declare the children born of this mamzerim. Hillel the Elder told the children: Bring me your mother's marriage contract. In it he found written: When you enter the wedding canopy, be my wife. So the children were not declared mamzerim.
13.why: The Gemara is listing Sages who drew legal conclusions from the everyday wording people used in their documents, after Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda; this is its example for Hillel.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: The Sage who reads the marriage contract and saves the children's status.

terms.meaning: Perform the first stage of Jewish marriage, which already makes a woman legally married to the man.
The chuppah, under which the second and final stage of the marriage takes place.
Children born of a forbidden union, such as between a married woman and another man. They and their descendants face lasting limits on whom they may marry.
The ketuba, the document a husband gives his wife at marriage, setting out his obligations to her.

14.note: A man leased land on the bank of the Malka Sava river to grow garlic, for a fixed sum of money. The river became dammed up. The case came before Rava, who told him that the Malka Sava does not usually dam up, so this was a regional disaster, and he could take the loss off his rent. The Rabbis objected to Rava from the mishna, where Rabbi Yehuda says one who leases for money never reduces the rent. Rava answered: No one is concerned for Rabbi Yehuda's view.
14.why: The mishna records Rabbi Yehuda's view that a fixed money rent is never cut for a regional disaster; this case shows Rava setting that view aside.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who lets the tenant reduce his rent.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage whose view in the mishna the Rabbis quote against Rava.

terms.meaning: A misfortune that strikes the whole area, not just one field. In such a case a tenant may pay less rent.
A passage of the Mishna, the first great written collection of Jewish law, which the Gemara then discusses.

15.note: A man leased land to grow hay, paying the owner a set number of kor of barley. After the field produced hay, he plowed it and sowed barley, and the barley was blighted. Rav Ḥaviva of Sura on the Euphrates sent the question to Ravina: is this like the mishna's case, where a tenant whose crop is blighted may pay from it? Ravina answered: Is it comparable? There the land failed to do what its owner leased it for; here the land did what its owner leased it for.
15.why: The mishna lets a tenant whose crop is blighted pay his rent from that crop; this case, and the soured-wine case after it, test how far that rule goes.

people.name: Rav Ḥaviva from Sura in the Euphrates
people.about: Sends the question to Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Answers that the case is not like the mishna's.

terms.meaning: A large measure of grain.
Struck by crop disease or a similar failure.

16.note: Rabbi Ami would announce that trees on both banks of a river must be cut back as wide as the shoulders of the men who pulled the boats. Rav Natan bar Hoshaya had sixteen cubits cut, and the people of Mashronya came and beat him. The Gemara explains that he thought the path should be as wide as a public road, sixteen cubits, but it only needs room for the pullers to stretch their ropes.
16.why: Rav Yehuda has just taught that the strip of land along a river belongs to everyone; this incident shows how much of the bank must be cleared for public use, and what happened to one who demanded too much.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Announces how far the trees must be cut back.

people.name: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya
people.about: Orders sixteen cubits cut and is beaten for it.

terms.meaning: Men who walked along the bank pulling boats upstream with ropes.
A measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip.
A public road or square, which in Jewish law is at least sixteen cubits wide.

17.note: Rabba bar Rav Huna had a forest on a riverbank. People told him to cut it down. He said: Let those above and below me along the river cut theirs first, and then I will cut mine. The Gemara asks how he could act this way, since a verse from Zephaniah teaches, as Reish Lakish explains it, that a person must first put himself in order and only then others.
17.why: Rabbi Ami has required trees along rivers to be cut back for the boat-pullers. The Gemara goes on to answer its question: the neighboring forest belonged to a Persian general, so cutting his own trees alone would achieve nothing.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the forest, who will not cut it before his neighbors do.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: His reading of the verse is quoted against Rabba bar Rav Huna.

18.note: Rabba bar Rav Naḥman was traveling by boat and saw a forest standing on the riverbank. He asked whose it was and was told it belonged to Rabba bar Rav Huna. He quoted a verse from Ezra: The hand of the princes and rulers has been first in this faithlessness. He told them: Cut it down, and they cut it down. Rabba bar Rav Huna came and found it cut, and he cursed: Whoever cut it, may his branches be cut down. It was said that for all the years of Rabba bar Rav Huna's life, the children of Rabba bar Rav Naḥman did not survive.
18.why: The Gemara has just explained that Rabba bar Rav Huna was within his rights to leave his trees, since cutting them alone would gain nothing; this story shows what came of acting against him.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Naḥman
people.about: Orders the forest cut down, and loses his children to the curse.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the forest, who curses whoever cut it.

19.note: Rav Pappa leased land to grow hay, and palm trees sprouted in it. When he left, he asked the owners to pay him for the added value. Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, asked whether he would also want paying if a palm tree simply grew thicker. Rav Pappa said that here, unlike there, he had taken the land expecting such gains. Rav Sheisha pressed: What did you lose, a handful of hay? Take it and go. Rav Pappa said he grows garden saffron. Rav Sheisha answered that he had shown he meant only to take his crop and leave: take your saffron and go; you get only the value of the wood.
19.why: The Gemara has been debating whether a tenant farmer is paid when a sycamore grows more valuable while he works the field, with Abaye saying yes and Rava no; it weighs Rav Pappa's claim against both views.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The tenant who asks to be paid for the palm trees.

people.name: Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi
people.about: Argues against Rav Pappa's claim.

terms.meaning: The added value a tenant's time on the land brought to the field, which he may sometimes claim when he leaves.
An expensive crop; Rav Pappa says the trees took up space he would have used for it.
What the palm trees would be worth cut down and sold as timber, much less than their worth as growing trees.

20.note: Rav Beivai bar Abaye leased land and put an earthen fence around it, and trees sprouted inside. When he left, he asked the owners to pay him for the added value. Rav Pappi said: Because you come from unfortunate people, you say unfortunate things? Even Rav Pappa claimed payment only where he suffered a loss; what loss do you have here?
20.why: It follows straight on Rav Pappa's claim for palm trees that sprouted in his leased field, and limits it: a tenant is paid for such growth only when it cost him something.

people.name: Rav Beivai bar Abaye
people.about: The tenant who asks to be paid for the trees.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Rejects his claim sharply.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: His earlier claim for sprouted palm trees is cited as the limit.

terms.meaning: The translation explains this as a jab at Abaye's family, said to descend from the priest Eli, whose descendants were fated to die young.
